title: Peshawar joins the kingdom
hook: the frontier city is brought into the kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir, and your line, the valley. Today we go west, to the other end of the map.

Peshawar is a market town where the plains run out. Caravans unload in its bazaars: horses, dried fruit, carpets from beyond the hills. Behind the city, the road climbs west toward Afghanistan. Traders came down that road. Armies came down it too, again and again, into the Punjab. A city at the mouth of a pass like that is never just a city. It's a door, and whoever holds it decides who comes in.
screen: `A CITY AT THE MOUTH OF A PASS.` → `TRADERS AND ARMIES.` → `A DOOR, NOT JUST A CITY.`

segments.voice: Peshawar didn't fall in a day. For years it sat between the Sikh kingdom and the Afghan rulers, paying tribute to Lahore at times, slipping back at others. Sikh histories tell of battles on the plains around it and the slow pull of the city toward Lahore. Then the general. You met him a few days ago: Hari Singh Nalwa, who held the frontier. As Sikh histories tell it, he brought Peshawar fully into the kingdom and then governed the region. He built forts, among them Jamrud near the pass, where he would later fall. With Peshawar held, the kingdom's edge sat at the foot of the Khyber. The door armies had used to come down into the Punjab was now held from Lahore, and Sikh tradition remembers it with pride: the invaders' road now had a Sikh guard on it. But a border city is never quiet. Peshawar had its own Pashtun leaders with their own loyalties, and the Afghan rulers wanted it back. Holding it meant troops, forts and constant watch. An edge is where a kingdom stands guard, and where it can be struck, both at once. A fort at the mouth of a pass, its gate facing the hills: that's the edge.
screen: `YEARS OF PULL BETWEEN TWO POWERS.` · `HARI SINGH NALWA BRINGS IT IN.` · `A SIKH GUARD ON THE INVADERS' ROAD.` · `AN EDGE IS STRONG AND EXPOSED.` · then, large: `THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Think of the edges of your own world: the last street you know well, the far side of your circle, the subject you always avoid. Pick one, rest your attention there for a few breaths without pushing past it, and notice how it feels to stand at the line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Peshawar, the city at the mouth of the Khyber, pulled toward Lahore for years and brought into the kingdom under Hari Singh Nalwa.
Your line: the edge. Every frontier is held one day at a time. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Why did holding Peshawar matter so much to the Sikh kingdom?
options: It sat at the mouth of the Khyber, the door invading armies had used.
It was the richest market around, and its taxes paid for the whole army.
It was where Guru Nanak was born, so the Maharaja wanted it for pilgrims.
chat.meaning: Peshawar sat where the Khyber road came down into the Punjab; holding it put a Sikh guard on the invaders' road.
